title: Letters & sounds
goal: What you see and what you hear are connected in different ways.

study.title: A letter is not a sound.
paragraphs: English has 26 letters. Speech uses a wider set of sound distinctions. Different accents and descriptions group those sounds differently, so there is no single sound count you need to memorize.
The same letter can represent different sounds. Several letters can represent one sound. A written letter can also be silent.
examples: The initial k is normally silent.
Again, you write k without a separate k sound.

paragraphs: Watch this introduction to English sounds. Listen, choose a sound, and try imitating it. You do not need to learn every symbol or pronunciation rule at once.

study.title: A map for pronunciation.
paragraphs: The International Phonetic Alphabet, or IPA, uses symbols for sounds. Letters such as a, b, and c belong to a writing system; symbols such as /æ/, /ʃ/, and /θ/ describe speech sounds.
A pronunciation entry can help when spelling alone is unclear. For example, /kæt/ shows the sounds in cat.
You can use the map without learning every part of it today.

study.title: Look. Listen. Try. Return.
paragraphs: Watch the model, listen carefully, and imitate a short part. Return to a sound or a song when you want another try.
For now, the useful discovery is that English spelling and sound are not a one-to-one match. The next lessons help you practice the movements more deliberately.
